blocks.text: A parcel is released at the top of a loading-dock chute tilted at 30 degrees. Will it slide, and how fast will it be moving at the bottom? The answer depends on a short drawing: one dot, three or four arrows, and a pair of axes. Mastering that drawing is the foundation of all of particle kinetics.

blocks.markdown: The **force-acceleration method** applies Newton's second law, $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$, directly to a particle. The method has three steps: (1) isolate the particle and draw a **free-body diagram** (FBD) showing every external force acting on it; (2) choose coordinate axes and write the component equations of motion; (3) solve, using kinematics or constraints if there are more unknowns than equations. Inertial effects appear only on the right-hand side as $ma$; the FBD itself never contains a force called $ma$.

blocks.title: Free-body diagram
blocks.text: A free-body diagram shows the particle isolated from its surroundings, with every external force on it drawn as an arrow at its point of application: the weight $m g$, contact forces from surfaces (normal reaction $N$ and friction $F$), tensions in strings, and applied forces. Forces the particle exerts on other bodies do not belong on its FBD.

blocks.caption: Components along chosen axes. $\mu_s$ and $\mu_k$ are the static and kinetic friction coefficients; friction opposes sliding.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing axes.** Pick axes that make the motion simplest. For a block on an incline, take $x$ **parallel** to the slope and $y$ **perpendicular** to it: the acceleration lies along $x$ and the perpendicular acceleration is zero, so $N=mg\cos\theta$ immediately. The weight resolves into $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into it. For a particle moving on a circle, use normal and tangential axes, with $\sum F_n=mv^2/r$ toward the centre.

blocks.title: Block sliding down a rough incline
blocks.prompt: A 20 kg block is released from rest on a plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal, with kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k=0.25$. Find its acceleration ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Perpendicular to the slope there is no acceleration, so find $N$.

blocks.answer: The block accelerates down the slope at $a\approx2.78$ m/s$^2$, equivalent to $g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)$.

blocks.markdown: When an applied force pulls the block, the friction force still opposes the sliding direction. If the block moves **up** the slope, both the downhill component of weight and kinetic friction act down the slope, so they both oppose the pull.

blocks.title: Crate hauled up a slope
blocks.prompt: A 50 kg crate is pulled up a $20^\circ$ incline by a rope parallel to the slope with tension 400 N. The kinetic friction coefficient is $\mu_k=0.30$. Find the acceleration ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Kinetic friction, directed down the slope.

blocks.answer: The crate accelerates up the slope at about 1.88 m/s$^2$.

rows: Mass on a string in a vertical circle
blocks.caption: Typical axes and equations of motion.

blocks.markdown: **Particle on a string in a vertical circle.** A bob of mass $m$ on a string of length $r$ moves on a vertical circle. At the lowest point the string tension $T$ points toward the centre (up) and the weight points away from it, so $T-mg=mv^2/r$. At the highest point both $T$ and $mg$ point toward the centre (down), so $T+mg=mv^2/r$. The tension is largest at the bottom and cannot be negative: the string goes slack if the speed at the top falls below $\sqrt{gr}$.

blocks.title: String tension at the bottom of the swing
blocks.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball on a 0.80 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 5.0 m/s. Find the tension there ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Draw the FBD: tension up (toward the centre) and weight down. Take upward as the normal direction.

blocks.answer: The tension is about 20.5 N, roughly four times the ball's 4.9 N weight.

items: Draw the particle alone and show every external force; label known values.
Choose axes that make one component of acceleration zero or known.
Write $\sum F=ma$ for each axis, with friction $F=\mu_kN$ if sliding.
Solve for $N$ first, then friction, then the acceleration.
Check signs, units (N, kg, m/s$^2$) and that the answer is physically reasonable.

blocks.title: Typical mistakes
blocks.text: Do not put $ma$ on the free-body diagram as a force. On an incline, $N$ is not $mg$: it is $mg\cos\theta$ when nothing else presses on the block. Friction opposes the sliding direction, so it changes sign when the block reverses. Always check that a computed tension is positive.

points: Newton's second law $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ is applied component-wise to a free-body diagram that shows all external forces on the particle.
On an incline, resolve parallel and perpendicular to the slope: $N=mg\cos\theta$ and $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)$ for sliding down.
For a string in a vertical circle, $T=m(g+v^2/r)$ at the bottom and $T=m(v^2/r-g)$ at the top, which must be non-negative.

questions.stem: Which of the following should appear on the free-body diagram of a block sliding down an incline?

options.text: Weight and the force the block exerts on the incline
Weight, normal reaction, friction and a force $ma$ down the slope

distractorRationale.a: Omits the contact forces from the surface.
distractorRationale.b: The force the block exerts on the incline acts on the incline, not on the block.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: all external forces on the block.
distractorRationale.d: $ma$ is the result of the forces, not a force.

questions.explanation: A free-body diagram contains only external forces acting on the isolated body. The quantity $ma$ is placed on the other side of Newton's second law, not drawn as a force.

questions.stem: A block rests on a rough incline at angle $\theta$ and is not accelerating perpendicular to the surface. The normal force from the incline is

distractorRationale.a: This is the weight component down the slope.
distractorRationale.b: Only true on a horizontal surface.
distractorRationale.c: Not obtained from either component equation.

questions.explanation: Resolving perpendicular to the slope, the only forces are $N$ and the component $mg\cos\theta$ of weight, and the acceleration is zero in that direction. Hence $N=mg\cos\theta$.

questions.stem: A block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at $30^\circ$. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, its acceleration down the slope is
questions.explanation: With no friction, the only force along the slope is $mg\sin\theta$, so $a=g\sin\theta=9.81\times0.5=4.905$ m/s$^2$. The mass cancels.

questions.stem: A block is on a rough incline with static friction coefficient $\mu_s=0.40$. The largest angle at which it can remain at rest is approximately

distractorRationale.a: This is the angle whose tangent is $1/\mu_s$ (complement).
distractorRationale.c: Confuses the friction coefficient with an angle in degrees.

questions.explanation: At the point of slipping $mg\sin\theta=\mu_smg\cos\theta$, so $\tan\theta=\mu_s=0.40$ and $\theta=21.8^\circ$. The mass cancels.

questions.stem: A small mass on a string of length 1.2 m is swung in a vertical circle. At the top its speed is 3.0 m/s. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, the equation $T+mg=mv^2/r$ would give a negative $T$. What does this mean?

options.text: The speed at the top must be 3.0 m/s greater
The string would go slack; the mass cannot follow the circular path at that speed
The string tension is directed outward

questions.correctOptionText: The string would go slack; the mass cannot follow the circular path at that speed

distractorRationale.a: The mass is accelerating toward the centre, not in equilibrium.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: $v^2/r=7.5<g$, so $T=m(7.5-9.81)<0$, impossible for a string.
distractorRationale.d: A string cannot push, so negative tension is not an outward force.

questions.explanation: Here $v^2/r=9/1.2=7.5$ m/s$^2$, which is less than $g$, so the weight alone exceeds the required inward force. A string can only pull, so $T\ge0$ is required; a negative result shows the mass leaves the circle.

questions.stem: A block slides down a $25^\circ$ incline with kinetic friction coefficient 0.15. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its acceleration in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Along the slope, $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)=9.81(0.4226-0.15\times0.9063)=9.81(0.2867)=2.81$ m/s$^2$. This is less than the frictionless value $g\sin25^\circ=4.15$ m/s$^2$, as expected.

questions.stem: A 0.80 kg bob on a 1.5 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 4.0 m/s. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the string tension there in newtons.
questions.explanation: At the bottom $T-mg=mv^2/r$, so $T=0.80(9.81+16/1.5)=0.80(9.81+10.67)=16.4$ N. This exceeds the bob weight of 7.85 N because the string must also supply the centripetal force.

questions.stem: A 12 kg crate is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 60 N. The kinetic friction coefficient is 0.30. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the acceleration of the crate in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Vertically $N=mg=117.7$ N, so friction is $0.30\times117.7=35.3$ N. Horizontally $60-35.3=12a$, giving $a=2.06$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem: Describe the steps of the force-acceleration method for a block sliding down a rough incline, and explain how the choice of axes simplifies the equations.
markingGuide: Draw an FBD of the block alone: weight, normal reaction, kinetic friction up the slope.
Choose $x$ along the slope and $y$ perpendicular to it.
Axes along the slope avoid resolving $N$ and $F$ and put the acceleration in a single axis.
questions.explanation: The FBD records the forces, and the chosen axes turn $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ into scalar equations where one has zero acceleration. This lets $N$ be found without solving simultaneous equations.

questions.stem: A bob of mass $m$ is whirled on a string of length $r$ in a vertical circle. Derive expressions for the tension at the lowest and highest points in terms of speed, and use them to find the minimum speed at the top for the string to remain taut.
markingGuide: Take the normal direction toward the centre of the circle.
Speed is higher at the bottom (energy exchange), so tension is greatest there.
questions.explanation: The same normal-direction equation gives opposite signs for the weight at the top and bottom because the centre lies on opposite sides. The slack condition $T=0$ gives the minimum speed $\sqrt{gr}$.
